title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and \(\Pr [A(F)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]\to 1\) as \(n\to \infty\) for F drawn from \(R_{3}(n,Cn)\)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
definitions: For \(n\ge 3, R_{3}(n,m)\) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and independently negates each of its three variables with probability \(1/2\). Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every \(\eta >0\) there is n0 such that the probability is at least \(1- \eta\) for all \(n\ge n0\). There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers \(C\ge 6\) loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

progress.text: Barak records a gap formulation of Feige’s hypothesis, requiring soundness on nearly satisfiable instances.
Allen–O’Donnell–Witmer give general random-CSP refutation algorithms and distinguish weak and strong refutation.
Chan–d’Orsi–Xu extend random-CSP refutation tradeoffs to predicates without uniformly random literals; the constant-density 3-SAT target is not established.

status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No sound polynomial-time refuter meeting the stated constant-density success guarantee was found. The exact-satisfiability variant must be distinguished from the stronger near-satisfiability formulations in the cited Feige-hypothesis literature.
review_note: The proposal’s explicit never-reject-a-satisfiable-instance condition is retained. This is not silently replaced by gap refutation. Classical randomization, exact soundness, distribution, input encoding and the order of quantifiers are fixed.

statement_review.reason: The target and computational model are explicitly specified. This is an editorial review, not a formal verification of the statement or cited proofs.
